extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers and practitioners (marketers, advertising strategists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for creating and assessing humorous advertisements so they attract attention and entertain without harming brand attitudes. Focuses on how humor-eliciting 'violations' (their severity, target, and motivational consequences) influence negative/positive affect and therefore brand outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation severity refers to the degree to which a violation threatens one’s well-being, identity, or normative belief structure — i.e., the degree to which the stimulus departs from consumers’ beliefs about how things should be. Violations vary on a continuum from no perceivable violation, to mild, to severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe violations are more difficult to appraise as benign and are more likely to elicit negative affect (anger, fear, disgust). Even when they produce perceived humor, severe violations tend to increase negative reactions and thus can hurt brand attitudes relative to milder violations. The authors operationalize severity three ways: (1) divergence from beliefs about how things should be, (2) whether the violation threatens a specific person/group vs people in general, and (3) whether the violation motivates avoidance rather than approach. Score/consider severity when choosing humorous content; prefer mild (benign) over severe violations when brand attitudes are an objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target of violation (inclusive vs exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations differ in whether they threaten a specific person or group (exclusive violations) or threaten people/society in general (inclusive violations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive violations single out a specific group or person (e.g., disparaging men or women) and are more likely to be perceived as mean-spirited, insulting, or politically incorrect, eliciting more negative affect and being riskier for brands. Inclusive violations (making fun of situations, humanity in general, or absurdities) are less likely to provoke negative feelings and can improve brand attitudes. Avoid humor that ridicules specific demographic or identity groups if brand health is a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral prompt / motivational tendency (avoidance vs approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some violations motivate avoidance (e.g., disgust, purity violations, shame, fear), whereas others motivate approach (e.g., anger, curiosity, confusion leading to engagement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations that prompt avoidance (especially purity/disgust-related content in food/drink categories) are more likely to reduce consumers' desire to approach or consume the product and are thus riskier for brand attitudes. When advertising consumables, avoid purity/impurity violations that could reduce purchase intent. Prefer approach-motivating violations when safe to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign appraisal requirement (benign violation theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when consumers simultaneously appraise a stimulus as a violation and as benign; a benign appraisal means the stimulus seems normative, acceptable, staged, hypothetical, inconsequential, or directed at a disliked character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke humor without provoking solely negative reactions, ensure violations can be appraised as benign — e.g., make violent or severe content appear staged, hypothetical, harmless, or applied to a disliked/fictional character. However, note that even benign-seeming severe violations can still increase negative affect and risk brand harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived humor alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful amusement (perceived humor) does not guarantee positive brand effects: ads can be found funny while simultaneously eliciting negative feelings that hurt brand attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on measures of funniness or laughter when evaluating humorous content. Assess both perceived humor and negative affect — an ad that is equally funny to another may produce worse brand outcomes if it elicits more negative feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative affect as mediator of brand harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative affective reactions (e.g., feeling offended, disgusted, uncomfortable) mediate the relationship between humorous violations and decreased brand attitudes and purchase intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing or pretesting humorous ads, measure negative affect explicitly (e.g., scales for offended, disturbed, disgusted) because increases in negative affect can explain decreases in brand attitude even when humor is present. Use mediation analysis to diagnose whether negative affect is driving adverse brand responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive affect role and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive affect (amusement, enjoyment) often accompanies humorous ads and may mediate beneficial effects, but positive affect does not always offset negative affect when both co-occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure positive affect (e.g., amused, funny, makes me laugh) as a control or potential mediator. In the studies, positive affect sometimes mediated differences in attitudes, but negative affect was a consistent predictor of harm; so both should be evaluated in tandem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of violations (categorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations can be categorized as physical, identity, communication/linguistic, social/cultural, or logic violations — each with distinct implications for perceived threat and benignness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the violation type when designing or coding ads: physical (harm/violence), identity (insults, stereotypes), communication/linguistic (puns, sarcasm), social/cultural (taboo topics, manners), logic (absurdities, impossibilities). Some types (e.g., purity/social taboos) are more likely to prompt avoidance and disgust and therefore pose greater brand risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding scales for evaluation (severity, withdrawal prompt, target)
rubrics_metrics.description: For systematic evaluation, the authors provide simple 3-point coding scales: Severity (1 mild – 3 severe), Withdrawal prompt (1 unlikely – 3 likely), Target (1 inclusive – 3 exclusive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ordinal scales when pretesting or auditing humorous ads to classify the violation and estimate risk. The 1–3 scales are designed for human coders and were used to predict which real humorous ads have more/less favorable brand effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual moderators (relevance, product category, argument strength, processing, need for levity, prior brand attitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of humor on brand attitudes depends on moderators such as the relevance of the humorous stimuli to the product, the product category, the strength of the ad's persuasive argument, consumers' level of processing, consumers' need for levity, and prior brand attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these contextual moderators when deciding whether to use humor: tailor humor to product relevance, be cautious with categories sensitive to particular violations (e.g., food and purity), and account for target consumers' preferences and prior brand views — humor can interact with these variables to change its effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-specific sensitivity (e.g., food/drink and purity violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain product categories (notably food and beverage) are especially vulnerable to violations that prompt disgust/purity concerns, which will reduce product preference and purchase intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid impurity/purity-related humor for consumable products. Pretest approach/avoidance tendencies (e.g., choice tasks) to detect whether an ad's violation decreases consumers' willingness to consume the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and selection criteria for evaluating real ads
rubrics_metrics.description: When assembling a sample of humorous print advertisements for evaluation, the authors required: the image depicts a print advertisement for a consumer product, brand name legible, and any copy in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If auditing a corpus of ads or conducting research, apply clear inclusion criteria to ensure comparability (format, legibility, language). This avoids confounds from unreadable copy or irrelevant ad types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement metrics used to evaluate humorous ads (scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evaluation used standardized multi-item scales: perceived humor (e.g., 'is humorous', 'makes me laugh', 'is funny'), positive affect scales, negative affect scales (e.g., offended, disturbed, disgusting), brand attitude scales (e.g., bad/good, unfavorable/favorable, negative/positive), and purchase intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pretesting or measuring effects, use validated multi-item scales and report reliability (α). Use both attitudinal (brand attitude) and behavioral/intention outcomes (purchase intent, product choice) to capture the real-world implications of humorous content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive, highly threatening, or avoidance-motivating humor (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor that targets a specific group, depicts highly inappropriate/severe violations, or elicits disgust/avoidance is prone to increase negative affect and harm brand attitudes even when perceived as funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical anti-pattern list: avoid (1) ridiculing specific demographic groups, (2) escalating severity to graphic or purity-related content for products where disgust matters, and (3) relying solely on shock or controversy to get attention without checking affective responses. Instead, prioritize mildly threatening, inclusive, and approach-motivating benign violations.
